utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. May I just return, before I begin, to the question of the admission of the transcript. I should, of course, make it clear, as I have indeed to my learned friends during the break, that they, of course, will have the perfect right to cross-examine on any matters. We're just asking for the admission, to get the general evidence in. Your Honour, before I begin, can I hand, having had a request from one of Your Honour's legal officers yesterday, can we hand to Your Honours copies of the documents that I'm going to be referring to in opening, although I will put them up on the ELMO. Your Honour, they are all documents that have been disclosed and given numbers, and those numbers have been written across the top so that Your Honours know where they are in the files. In addition, there are some maps which Your Honours may wish to have at this stage, and I'll refer to them. The interpreters, I think, have been given copies of the documents already, and the Defence. Yes. Your Honours, may I begin my address to Your Honours by dealing in general terms with the allegations that the Prosecution make against the accused Milomir Stakic in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Those allegations arise out of the events which took place in the municipality of Prijedor, which is in north-west Bosnia, between April and September of 1992. In the ten years since the conflict in Bosnia started, Prijedor has already become notorious for reflecting at the highest and most concentrated level, all the crimes that were committed under the, as it's now become known, the term "ethnic cleansing." And I say again, there is no such crime as "ethnic cleansing." What it describes is a course of criminal conduct. The events have in part already been the subject of earlier cases. The first case ever heard before this Tribunal, that of Tadic, Kvocka and others, known generally as the Omarska case. Sikirica and others, concerning the camp at Keraterm. And the trial of Kovacevic, which would have, had it continued to its final conclusion, dealt with the same type of events and the same type of authority, but because Kovacevic died, the trial was never concluded. He was, as Your Honours will hear, intimately connected with this accused. The crimes involved at their lowest the denial to non-Serbs of their rights to employment, to freedom of movement, to medical care, and to proper judicial process. The denial of those rights was just the beginning of a process. That process escalated into attacks on villages and areas occupied by non-Serbs, with the consequent loss of civilian life, the destruction of property, and in particular, the deliberate targeting of institutions dedicated to religion. Those not killed during the course of the attacks were rounded up and incarcerated in what were called, in yet another euphemism, "detention facilities" or reception centres or collection centres. In those camps - because that is what they were - mass murder was committed. Individuals were beaten, resulting sometimes in death. Torture was commonplace, and sexual assaults took place on a regular basis. Conditions in those camps, that is to say, the provision of food, water, medical care, were inadequate, to say the least. Those released from the camps, and others, were deported in the thousands, forcibly deported from areas in which their families had lived for decades, if not generations. And this, say the Prosecution, was the ultimate goal of all of these crimes, in other words, to remove, through the commission of these crimes, the non-Serb population from the municipality of Prijedor. The actual physical perpetration of the crimes was carried out by members of the Bosnian Serb army, which includes the territorial forces; the police forces; and effectively, ordinary Bosnian Serbs, who put on uniform, formed themselves into paramilitary groups, whether on a small or a larger scale, and turned upon their non-Serb neighbours with whom they had lived in harmony and indeed had intermarried between the various ethnicities. They did so with a ferocity which is only explicable within the climate of fear and hatred, which was deliberately created by those who were in a position to incite or instigate and thereafter control the course of events. Who were those people? In the municipality of Prijedor itself, the Prosecution say that they were the political and military leaders in positions of authority within that municipality. People such as this accused, Milomir Stakic. The original co-defendants on this indictment which he now faces alone: Milan Kovacevic, with whom I have already dealt, who was president of the Executive Board of the municipal assembly when it existed, and also a member of the Prijedor Crisis Staff; a man called Simo Drljaca, another name that lives in infamy who was at the time chief of the police in Prijedor. As is well known, he was killed when resisting the lawful arrest of himself some years ago. Men like Lieutenant Colonel, later Colonel Arsic, and his second in command, Major Zeljaja, both of whom represented the military presence in the Prijedor area. The military and political wings of the Bosnian Serbs were inextricably linked. The political wing provided the goal, the military and the police, who straddled the divide between the two arms, played their part in the achievement of these goals through the attacks, through the staffing which was provided for the camps already mentioned. The police's role encompassed both civilian action, carrying out the political orders that non-Serbs should be disarmed, the arrests of what were called undesirable personnel, the interrogations of those who were detained, but they also played a part in the military, because they raised battalions of fighting men. However, the accused and the others already mentioned in the municipality of Prijedor who had authority there did not act in isolation. The Prijedor Crisis Staff, which was headed by the accused, had close links with the regional Crisis Staff of the autonomous region of Krajina, headed by Radoslav Brdjanin, who also stands trial in this court. Major Zeljaja and Lieutenant Colonel Arsic were reporting to General Talic, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, based in Banja Luka, which was the military corps covering the area. General Talic stands trial together with Radoslav Brdjanin. Simo Drljaca was reporting to the chief of the CSB, the acronym for the Bosnian language but which is effectively the regional police headquarters. That was in Banja Luka, and the head of the CSB was Stojan Zupljanin, also indicted, not yet arrested. Both Momir Talic and Zupljanin were on the Crisis Staff that was covering the regional area of the autonomous region of Krajina. Moreover, the events in Prijedor were not unique to that municipality. In some form or other, the same features, the same crimes, occurred in other municipalities, particularly those that had no overall Serb majority of the inhabitants but contained a substantial proportion of Serbs. The Prosecution say that this is no coincidence but happened as a matter of design. The evidence will show that the Bosnian Serb leadership, ranging from the very top, at the republic level, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Plavsic through the leaders of what became known as the Serb autonomous regions, one of which was the autonomous region of Krajina, and down at the very least, the level of the municipality leaders. All of these people were acting together in furtherance of a common design or enterprise or plan, whichever expression one wishes to use. What was that design? The Prosecution say, on the evidence of what was said, what was written, and what was done, the design was the intention to permanently remove the non-Serb population from areas which had been designated as part of a Serbian state within Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that permanent removal was to be effected by the commission of the crimes set out in this indictment. We stress: It is important not to confuse motive, which was the creation of this Serbian state, with the intention, which I have just referred to, namely, that that Serbian state was to be created by the commission of crimes. The Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats were the object of these crimes for no other reason than their ethnicity. In Prijedor, there was a higher proportion of Muslims than Croats, and therefore the majority of the evidence in this case will concern the crimes that were committed against the Muslims. They formed the larger proportion of the victims in this case. It was clear as far back as October of 1991 what was intended by the Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs. Karadzic made it crystal clear in a speech that he made to the SDS, and I'm going to ask that at this stage a clip from that speech is played to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "You Muslims are not ready for war. You could face extinction." That was said by Karadzic in 1991, October, and in the course of 1992, that is what the Bosnian Serbs set out to achieve. The Prosecution suggest that once the evidence has been heard, the Court can and will be satisfied that the crime of persecutions, as set out in count 6, was committed by the accused acting in concert with others. However, the Prosecution goes further. On the evidence, the ferocity of the methods we used in Prijedor, the non-Serb populations, the scale of killings which took place, the targeting, selection for imprisonment and killing of persons thought to be leaders, the attacks upon and destruction of villages, homes, and religious institutions, the level of violence inside and outside the camps. The Prosecution say that all of this demonstrates an intention to destroy, at least in part, the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat population in Prijedor, in other words, the most serious crime of all, genocide. The Prosecution alleges that Milomir Stakic is criminally liable for genocide because either he intended the destruction of the non-Serb population in order to fulfil the aims and objectives of the criminal enterprise, where persecutions would be insufficient to achieve the desired result. Alternatively, on the basis that the natural and foreseeable consequence of the criminal enterprise, if you come to the conclusion that such an enterprise did exist, was that genocidal conduct, with the requisite intent, would be committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think there's a problem with the translation in the French booth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Can you make a test, please, the French cabin?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's working now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I was doing was setting out the alternative basis on which, if Your Honours were satisfied that an enterprise, a criminal enterprise existed, and that it was a foreseeable and natural consequence of that enterprise that genocidal conduct, with the requisite intent, would be committed, and Stakic was aware that such a result might ensue but nonetheless continued, deliberately and in full knowledge, with his part in that enterprise, then again, he would be guilty of the crime of genocide. Or finally, as a superior, within the meaning of Article 7(3), Stakic knew or had reason to know that genocidal conduct was about to be committed with genocidal intent and failed to take any steps to prevent or punish. I said finally. There is one final possibility, and that is as an aider and abetter, he knew that his principals were committing genocidal conduct with the requisite intent. But in effect, the Prosecution suggests that the first two are the real bases on which Stakic is guilty of genocide. Your Honour, those are the allegations in the most general of terms. Before turning to some detail, can I just quickly outline, so that it's clear, what the purpose of this opening is, and can I start with a negative. It's not going to be a complete rehearsal of the evidence. Your Honours have all seen the pre-trial brief which sets out that evidence. Your decision, of course, will be arrived at on the evidence and not what we say about it in advance or even at the end of the day, or indeed, in their turn, what the Defence have to say. It's upon the evidence that you reach your decisions. And above all, other than what I have already said in terms of genocide, because it is only right that the accused should hear how we put the case, it is not going to be a submission of law on all the elements of the various offences charged. What we intend to do at this stage is to present an overview of the evidence it is anticipated will be given, and I emphasise the word "anticipated." It may be known to Your Honours that whatever witnesses may have said in statements, very often the witness will give an account which differs. Your Honours will no doubt bear in mind that for each and every one of the witnesses, the victims, these events occurred ten years ago. These were events, on any showing, of a traumatic nature, and memories fade, or in other words, things -- another example is things become magnified in a way that they might not at the time. There will also be evidence from what can generally be described Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. as people coming into an expert category, and some from outsiders who visited the area at the time. The description that I'm going to deal with now of the evidence ultimately involves a selection. In the massive documentation that goes with this case and in the massive witness statements, we have to make a selection. Because I omit at this stage a particular aspect of the evidence does not mean that it is not considered to be important. In the end, what is important, what is not important, will, in any event, be a matter for Your Honours. This opening is intended as a guide to the evidence that will be called. I propose to deal with the background to these events, then the chronology, which will include various, as it were, themes or aspects, the killings and the camps, the attacks; and finally, the role of Stakic himself in all of these events. Your Honours, can I start with the background. The Prijedor municipality, as I've already said, is situated in north-west Bosnia. If Your Honours could take the map, one of the small ones. I need to ask that it be put up on the ELMO as well. Yes. Thank you. If you could zoom in on it. Your Honours can see Prijedor marked in green and then the rest of the surrounding municipalities. Banja Luka, which is one of the bigger municipalities bordering Prijedor, was in effect the seat of the Serbian government in north-west Bosnia. Sanski Most, moving round, which you can see, again had a substantial proportion of Muslims within that municipality, and like Prijedor, was the subject of extreme violence, killings, and camps. Bosanski Novi bordered with Croatia, as did Bosanska Dubica and Bosanska Gradiska, all of those being municipalities which bordered with Prijedor. And Prijedor was of some importance because of its position. As Your Honours will hear, particularly during the conflict in Croatia it was the route by which troops went through from Banja Luka and other places towards the areas of Croatia in which fighting was taking place. The census which was taken in 1991 recorded -- and perhaps if Your Honours look at document 7, which is the first of the documents that we provided you with. It's not translated because it's fairly clear. Prijedor is shown at the bottom. The first column is the total number of inhabitants in each municipality that's shown. The next column shows the Croats. The next column shows the Muslims, the Serbs, people who described themselves then as Yugoslav, and finally, others, apparently including Hungarians and other east European nationalities. One goes down to Prijedor, one can see that the total number of inhabitants in 1991, we have the census 1971, 1981, and 1991, was just over 112.000 people. Of that total, 6.300-odd were Croat, 49.300-odd were Muslims, or I should say declared themselves for the purposes of the census. 47.500-odd declared themselves to be Serb, and then 6.000-odd -- six-and-a-half-thousand-odd Yugoslav and just over 3.000, others. So the Muslims had a slight majority over the Serbs, and if added together with the Croats, had a much greater majority. The Serbs were clearly not in a majority in Prijedor. Can I ask Your Honours then to look at the map that's headed "Prijedor ethnic composition." That has been produced by the. You will see the composition -- yes. Maybe it better be put on the ELMO, although it won't fit entirely, but we can try. If we can just -- I'm sorry, usher. If you can just go to the side. Yes. It shows the ethnic composition in 1991. The figures shown from 1995 are taken from a Serb-produced document. One can see the distribution -- if we could move the map, sorry, on the ELMO slightly. Thank you. The distribution of the Muslim villages Hambarine, Biscani, and the like; the Serb areas around Omarska and up towards the north of the municipality; and the Croat area bordering the area with Croatia. Your Honours, we'll come back -- those names may already be familiar from the indictment, but we'll come back to them as we deal with the events. Yes, thank you very much. Now, in November of 1990, the first multiparty elections were held, and they were held across Yugoslavia. In Bosnia, three main parties emerged: The SDS, which was the Serb party; the SDA, which was the Muslim party; and the HDZ, which was the Croat. There were also other smaller parties that won seats. In Prijedor, the SDA won the largest number of seats in the municipal assembly. The municipal assembly was the highest governmental organ within the municipality. However, already at this early stage of events, the SDS resisted the allocation of positions, which was consistent with the election results. 1991 saw the beginning of the break-up of Yugoslavia. On the 25th of June of 1991, Slovenia and Croatia, following a referendum in each of their respective republics, declared their independence. In Slovenia, the JNA left the Yugoslav People's Army after a ten-day war. But in Croatia, the conflict between the JNA, assisted by various paramilitary organisations, and the Croatian forces lasted until January of 1992. And then as a result of international pressure, the JNA largely withdrew into Bosnia. The war in Croatia had a significant impact in Prijedor. In September of 1991, the Prijedor territorial organisation, then called the 5th Kozara Partizan Brigade which later became absorbed into the Bosnian Serb army, the VRS, was mobilised and it was deployed to western Slavonia, the area of Croatia close to the border. In addition, as I've already stated, troops going to and from Croatia would pass through the municipality. The SDA throughout Bosnia did not generally support the mobilisation which took place, but nonetheless, within Prijedor, a certain number of Muslims did respond to mobilisation and did join the army. The clearly inevitable break-up of the Federal Republic o Yugoslavia was anthema to the Serbs, particularly those in Bosnia, and in 1991, if not earlier, they planned to establish Serb-controlled territories within Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the area of north-west Bosnia, later to become the Autonomous Region of Krajina, which as I've said also included Prijedor, in April of 1991, an organisation calling itself the Association of the Municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina was formed. On the face of it, it was an association designed for economic cooperation. It had its own assembly. But the municipalities which joined that association were those with a predominantly Serb population. The decision to join had to be made by each municipal assembly. Prijedor did not have a majority of Serbs in the assembly, and so it did not join at that stage in 1991. By September of 1991, the aims and the purpose of this association had become much clearer because it transformed itself into the Autonomous Region of Krajina Assembly. On the 24th of October, 1991, the Bosnian Serb leadership established the Assembly of the Serb people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. One of the first actions of that assembly was to call for a plebiscite of Serbs in Bosnia on the question of whether they wished to remain in the Yugoslav federal state. That plebiscite took place on the 9th and 10th of November of 1991, with the results, as reported by the SDS, in any event, being overwhelmingly in favour of so remaining. And on the 21st of November of 1991, the assembly passed a resolution declaring that all territories where Serbs had voted in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia were part of the Yugoslav Federation, and at that stage it also verified the five Serb Autonomous Regions, the SAOs, again a title in the Bosnian language, which had been declared and which included the Krajina. I should add that Krajina means no more in the Bosnian language than border, and one of the things to be aware of as the evidence progresses is that there was the Krajina in Bosnia and there was also the Croatian Krajina, known generally as the RSK. On the 9th of January, 1992, the assembly proclaimed the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This entity was said to consist of the autonomous regions and, as it was put, other Serb ethnic areas. How were those Serb ethnic areas defined? They were defined as those in which Serbs had voted to remain in Yugoslavia and those in which the Serbs were a minority as a result of the genocide committed against them in World War II, and this seems to have some bearing on the municipality in Prijedor, which was the subject of atrocities during the course of a war that had finished some nearly 50 years before that. In Prijedor, following the multiparty elections of 1990, a Muslim, a member of the SDA named Muhamed Cehajic - I hope that's the right pronunciation - was elected president of the assembly. The accused was elected the vice-president, and Milan Kovacevic became the president of the Executive Committee of the assembly, which had considerable powers. Other appointments, particularly those connected with the police, were an ongoing source of friction between mainly the SDA and SDS. In September of 1991, a man named Simo Miskovic had been elected president of the SDS in Prijedor, and Stakic vice-president. And on the 20th of September, the SDS issued a statement accusing the SDA of colluding with the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo to smuggle arms into Kozarac whilst the SDA had interim control of all the police positions while the arguments continued, Kozarac being a particular Muslim area. And Stakic himself then claimed that there was a Serb majority if Prijedor and three neighbouring municipalities were taken together. The Prosecution will say on the evidence that Stakic was fully committed to the Serb, the SDS, ideology and plan. On the 19th of December of 1991, the SDS issued a document which was headed "Instructions for the organisation and activity of the organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina." It has become known as the Variant A and Variant B document, and it is worth having a look at that. It's document 201 -- no. What's happened to it? I don't know whether Your Honours -- no. Your Honours, I'm sorry. It's the one document that I seem to have left behind. Can I tell Your Honours, and I will come back to it if I may after the break whenever we take, because it's important and I think Your Honours should look at it and I see I've left it out of the pile although I needed it. Your Honours, there are a number of different versions of this particular -- do Your Honours have document 39? I think it must have just gone from my bundle. Your Honours, there are a number of different versions of this document which have been acquired by the Office of the Prosecutor. It's just been drawn to my attention that I attached another document to it. The one that in fact I think has been disclosed and in fact is contained by Dr. Donia's report is number 96, but copy 100 has a marginally better translation. The reason there are a number of copies is they were clearly distributed and I'm going to show why we can say that in a moment, to the various local boards of the SDS. Your Honours, if one looks at the first page of the document, Your Honours will see that in paragraph 2: "The tasks, measures, and other activities described in these instructions will be undertaken in order to enhance the preparedness of the Serbian people and its readiness to defend its interests." The tasks, measures, and other activities described in these Instructions shall be implemented on the entire territory of the socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina i.e., in all the municipalities inhabited by the Serbian people, to wit: In their entirety, in municipality where the Serbs are a majority (Variant "A") and partially in municipalities where the Serbs are not a majority (Variant "B")." And Prijedor was a Variant B municipality. Paragraph 4: "In order to ensure uniform and timely implementation, the tasks, measures, and other activities shall be implemented in Variants A and B, each consisting of two stages." Your Honours, if one goes to Variant B, which begins on the fifth page, it sets out the first stage of the activities. Round-the-clock staffing in all SDS municipal boards, creating conditions for daily meetings of the secretariats of SDS municipal boards. "(3) The SDS municipal board shall immediately form a Crisis Staff of the Serbian people in the municipality to be composed of --" and it then sets out the composition of the Crisis Staff and says "that the president of the municipal board of the SDS will be the commander of the Crisis Staff." It goes on to say: "The commander shall appoint a member of the Crisis Staff to coordinate relations with the municipal leaderships of the SDA and the HDZ." Well, that never seems to have happened. Paragraph 4 of the instructions: "Convene and proclaim an assembly of the Serbian people in the municipality, composed of Serbian assemblymen in the municipal assembly and chairmen of the local SDS boards." Then it goes on to deal with the setting up of the state organs in the municipality, "prepare," in the second part of paragraph 5: "Prepare the takeover of staff and selected equipment of Security Services centres." Item 6, "setting up secret storage places and depots for the storage of foodstuffs and other articles in short supply." That, we suggest on the evidence, was interpreted to mean weaponry. And then again in the second part of paragraph 6: "The Crisis Staff shall have exclusive authority over the organisation and supervision of these tasks." If one then goes to the second stage, and there we see, other than convening a session of the Serbian Municipal Assembly, paragraph 2: "Mobilise all Serbian members of the police forces and, in cooperation with JNA commands and staffs, ensure their gradual resubordination." The implementation of the order to mobilise, protection of buildings and facilities, and then, later on, in paragraph 6: "At the approaches to places inhabited by Serbs, organise covert surveillance and set up a system for reporting all possible threats to the Serbian population. In this connection, plan appropriate protection measures and prepare for a possible transfer of people and material goods to safer regions and areas." And finally, 7: "Special defence measures to be implemented in the municipalities where Serbs are not in a majority shall be the responsibility of the Crisis Staff, which shall constantly monitor the situation in the municipality, while also following broader political, military, and security developments. The Crisis Staff shall also initiate and carry out activities appropriate to any given situation and its possible development." How was that interpreted in Prijedor? As Your Honours will see, it was interpreted to mean the takeover by the SDS of all the organs of authority within the municipality. Now, I said, Your Honours, it was clear this was distributed, this document, to the various municipal SDS boards, and one can see that quite clearly from the next document, document 40, which is taken from the book of minutes of the meeting of the Prijedor municipal board of the SDS held on the 27th of December, 1991. There we can see that the agenda consisted of the implementation of the decision and enactment of the positions adopted by the assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then under the item small 1, president of the Prijedor SDS municipal board, one can see President Miskovic then read out the instruction delivered to the Prijedor municipal board of the SDS by the Serbian assembly. And one can see under there the various factors that I've just gone through listed: The establishment of an assembly of the Serbian people in Prijedor; mobilising the police, the TO; security for important facilities; and just so there be no doubt about this, and I say this, Your Honour, because this has been the subject of some considerable argument in various other trials in this building, Variant II, B crossed out, and then the first variant. And then: "After the presentation of the instruction, Miskovic gave a briefing on what has been done." And then over the page, one sees the meaning and purpose of forming municipal crisis staffs and local crisis staffs in the municipality was explained. Further down the page, effectively the composition of the Crisis Staff, again repeating the instructions, because item 3 says: "The president of the Prijedor municipal board of the SDA is the Crisis Staff commander." And finally, there was a scheduling, the date for the assembly of the Serbian people, and Stakic, so it was quite clear that he was present, suggesting the 3rd of January, and there was some argument about the date. And then at the bottom of the page, the persons who were to set committees, and the committee for social affairs, Milomir Stakic. Now, Your Honour, the discussion of the date on which it took place, that seems to have comes closest to Mr. Dusac's suggestion although later on proclamation on the 7th of January, because indeed the first meeting of the Serbian assembly of Prijedor met on the 7th of January, 1992. It is necessary to emphasise this was not an elected assembly. It set itself up parallel to and in opposition to the elected municipal assembly. The Serbian assembly elected Stakic as its first president, not all together clear why it wasn't Miskovic, however. And one of the first things that the assembly did, on the 17th of January - and this is document number 69 - was to make a decision to unite with the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina. The Serbian people assembly of the Prijedor municipality unanimously passes a decision on uniting the Serbian territories in the Prijedor municipality with the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, and it was signed on the original and had a stamp by the accused. Now, from then on, that is, January of 1992, ethnic tensions in Prijedor began to rise. Those tensions were fueled by speeches made by SDS politicians, including Stakic, and propaganda being broadcast on the TV and radio. As far back as August of 1991, the TV transmitter on Mount Kozara had been seized by Bosnian Serb extremists, including a rather well-known paramilitary criminal group called the Wolves of Vucak headed by a man called Milenkovic. As a result of that seizure, no broadcasts could be received in the Prijedor area, or indeed many other areas, including Banja Luka, from Sarajevo or anywhere other than Serb-controlled areas, such as Belgrade, Banja Luka itself, and Novi Sad. And what was pumped out from television and radio was propaganda designed to make the ordinary Serbs believe that they were under threat of genocide, of murders, of killings from their non-Serb neighbours. Witnesses will tell Your Honours about a steady build-up of military activity in the area. Arms and weapons were -- arms and weapons were supplied to Serbian villages and areas in the municipality. A referendum was held in February of 1992 seeking assent for the declaration of an independent Bosnian state. The SDS instructed Serbs to boycott that referendum, and for the most part they did, and the result of the referendum was a vote in favour of that declaration of independence, and that added further fuel to the fires that were being stoked up in the Prijedor area. In March and April of 1992, Serb checkpoints began to be set up in the municipality, and the final spark which ignited the conflict came with the recognition of that independence of Bosnia on the 6th of April, 1992. It did not take long for that ignition to lead to full-scale activity. On the 30th of April, 1992, the Serbs seized power in Prijedor. Non-Serb policemen were forced to hand over their weapons to their Serb colleagues. Serb flags flew from the official buildings and Radio Prijedor broadcast the news that the Serbs had taken over the municipality, rather like the lunatics taking over the asylum. Stakic, accompanied by men in uniform, went to the radio station to explain that the SDS had seized power. That same day, it was announced that a Crisis Staff had been formed in Prijedor and would be in charge of all activities. That was merely a formal announcement of an event which had already taken place earlier but had been confined at that stage within the SDS. Your Honours, because the fact of a Crisis Staff is of such importance, I should take a few minutes to explain what a Crisis Staff is. I don't know whether Your Honours would want to take a break at this stage or at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we should now have a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can resume five minutes past 12.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was about to deal with the topic of Crisis Staffs and what they were or appear to be. Your Honours, we saw that the Variant A and B document instructed the SDS boards to set up crisis staffs, and we saw the implementation in Prijedor. In fact, those instructions were followed by the SDS leaders in all ARK municipalities and also at the regional level of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Now, at various stages, these crisis staffs were called or renamed war staffs or war presidencies, but the essence of the body remained the same, and throughout this case it will be referred to as the Prijedor Crisis Staff. The concept of a Crisis Staff appears to have been derived from the laws of National Defence enacted in both the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and within Bosnia itself, and that allowed such a body or the presidency to perform all the functions which an assembly could perform during, and I quote, "a state of war or in the event of immediate danger of war." Now, once the state of emergency or the war was over, and an example known to witnesses was there was an earthquake in the Banja Luka Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. area in 1969. That was a national emergency and the Crisis Staff was set up to deal with that. But once the state of emergency or the war situation was over, any decrees made by this War Presidency or Crisis Staff would have to be submitted when the assembly first met again for ratification, and that indeed, for what it was worth, was what happened in this case at the conclusion of the Crisis Staff, the decisions it had made were submitted to the Serb Municipal Assembly for verification, and likewise, at the regional level, the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was asked to ratify decisions taken by the Krajina Crisis Staff. Now, the Crisis Staffs which were formed consisted of members drawn from the assembly and other leading figures. If one looks at document 168, and I think I'm going to ask for it to be put up on the ELMO, so that the accused can see. Yes. This was published in the Official Gazette of the Prijedor municipality and it relates to a meeting of the 22nd of May of 1992, the decision on appointment to the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff. The following are hereby appointed to the posts of President, Vice-president, and members. To the post of President, Dr. Stakic, President of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, that is to say, the Serb assembly. Vice-president, Mr. Savanovic who was vice-president of the Municipal Assembly. Dr. Milan Kovacevic, president of the executive committee of the Prijedor municipality. To the post of member, Slobodan Kuruzovic commander of the municipal Territorial Defence staff, a name that will come up again in connection with the camps. Bosko Mandic, commander of the Prijedor civil defence staff, to the post of member, Drljaca, Simo, chief of the Prijedor public security station. Slavko Budimir, secretary of the Prijedor municipal secretariat for People's Defence, and so on and so forth. And on the second page, one can see the decision was signed by Dr. Stakic. Yes, thank you. The military, if not actually officially members of the ARK -- sorry -- the Prijedor Crisis Staff played a part in the meetings. The Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region, and all the municipal Crisis Staffs, were inextricably linked in a symbiotic relationship. On the 18th of May of 1992, and that is document 166, and I don't think we need bother to put it up, if Your Honours have it - you will see what's headed "conclusions," and there, under item 2, it is declared that the Crisis Staffs are now the highest organs of authority in the municipalities, and that decisions was signed by the president of the Crisis Staff, Radoslav Brdjanin. He was the exception to the rule that the head of the Serbian assemblies that were set up became president of the Crisis Staffs because he in fact had become the vice-president of the assembly of the Autonomous Region. So on the 18th of May, the Crisis Staffs were declared to be the highest organs of authority in the municipalities, and if one looks at the next document, 176, which is a conclusion reached on the 26th of May, 1992 by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region, item 1, or conclusion 1: "The work of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region has absolute support, since it is now the highest organ of authority in the Autonomous Region, as the Assembly of the Autonomous Region cannot function due to objective and subjective circumstances, unspecified. Decisions of the Crisis Staff are binding for all Crisis Staffs in the municipalities. These decisions of the Crisis Staff shall be submitted for verification to the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina as soon as it is able to convene." The ARK Crisis Staff issued instructions to the municipal Crisis Staffs and in its turn, the municipal Crisis Staff issued its instructions. The nature of the relationship between the Crisis Staff and the other organs of government - for example, the police - can be seen in yet another example, a document this time marked 169, which was a dispatch from the Banja Luka Security Services Centre, the CSB, sent to all chiefs of departments of the security centres and all public security stations in the region except Jajce, the reason being that Jajce was Muslim-controlled. It dealt with conclusions reached at a meeting held on the 6th of May and attended, if one looks at the first page, by the chiefs of -- and there's a list of places, and on the -- about the eighth line you will see Prijedor attending the meeting. In this document, which was signed by Stojan Zupljanin, the chief of the CSB, there was a paragraph, number 23 -- if we go to page 6 of the document: "In all our activities, we must observe all measures and apply all procedures ordered by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region. With regard to disarmament, when the time set as the deadline for weapon surrender expires on the 11th of May, 1992, we must refrain from doing anything about it until the Crisis Staff passes relevant decisions." It is part of the Prosecution's case that that order to disarm, couched in non-specific terms in the sense of who it was aimed at, was aimed only at the non-Serb population, and it was that ultimatum which directly gave the excuse to the Serbs to start attacks on the non-Serb villages and areas. The hierarchy of authority, effectively republic to regional to municipal, wasn't as rigid as all of that. At times clearly directives would go directly from the republic level to the municipal level. There was still the chain of command within the Ministry of the Interior and the police and the like. But something of the nature of the Crisis Staff and its powers can be seen from the instructions that the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff issued in June of 1992 for the establishment and workings of the local Crisis Staffs, to which reference had been made in the original Variant A and B document. The Prosecution suggest that they clearly demonstrate the extent of the control that was exercised by the body known as the local Crisis Staff. The first page is the general provisions and says where these local crisis staffs are to be set up, the various areas and villages. And then on page 3, one can see the rights and duties, which by implication, we suggest, were the same duties carried out at a higher level at the municipal level to exercise and coordinate authority, maintain effective protection and defence of the local territory, to control the security of the territory, to maintain constant synchronisation and coordination of the measures of the action of the military and the police in the local area, to develop the most varied forms and methods of information and political propaganda activities, to organise and revive the economy, and so on and so forth. At paragraph 8, over the page, the local Crisis Staffs are to report to the Prijedor Crisis Staff and keep it regularly informed on the situation and the problems in the field and in their work, and again, by extension, the Prijedor municipality reported to the ARK Crisis Staff. Then paragraph 11, the local crisis staffs are to carry out other work in accordance with the decisions and other documents passed by the Assembly, the Presidency, government of the Serbian Republic, competent organs of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the Prijedor municipality Crisis Staff. And then the composition of the local Crisis Staff. And then, over the page, the duties of the local Crisis Staff members. And it sets out the Crisis Staff president managing the work of staff, responsible for the following: Implementation and coordination of staff decisions and conclusions; establishment and maintenance of contacts with the municipal Crisis Staff; provision of information to the municipality; implementation of its decisions, conclusions, and orders, and so on and so forth. Any suggestion that may be made that the head of the Crisis Staff was without power, the Prosecution suggest is a nonsense. Your Honours, can I now turn to the events, in brief, that took place in the municipality of Prijedor. During the weeks which followed the takeover on the 30th of April, Radio Prijedor repeatedly broadcast demands that non-Serbs identify their homes by marking their exteriors with something white. Non-Serbs, as a result of the orders issued by the Crisis Staff in the Autonomous Region, and repeated and reinforced by the Prijedor Crisis Staff, were ordered to surrender all their weapons, even those for which a licence was held. This order was not implemented in respect of Serbs. They were able to retain their weapons, and even more so, were being supplied with new weapons. Movement for non-Serbs became increasingly restricted. Dismissals of non-Serbs from employment took place on an increasing basis. In particular, there was what appeared to be a targeting of those in professional or managerial posts. Their Serb replacements were specifically instructed by the Prijedor authorities to submit information on what was called the levelling of cadres. If Your Honours look very briefly at document 167. This in fact was a conclusion signed this time by the chairman of the executive committee, Milan Kovacevic. It appears that certain powers were delegated to the executive committee, and there one sees "Newly appointed acting directors of companies, factories, and institutions must inform the executive committee as to the changes, in particular, production and finance, and the levelling of cadres." That, we suggest, was another euphemism. What it actually meant was the dismissal of non-Serb employees. It became clear to the non-Serb population that they were, to say the least, at risk. In the Kozarac area, which Your Honours can look again at the map, was predominantly Muslim, there was a refusal to hand over weapons because they feared, as it turned out, with justification, that they were, as it were, ripe to be attacked. On the 22nd of May, there was a short and small but violent incident. The Muslims, in response to the Serb checkpoints and because of their fear that they were going to be attacked, had set up themselves a checkpoint at one of the entrances to the villages of Hambarine. During this incident, two Serbs were killed and some others were injured. As a result, an ultimatum was issued by Serb officials including Stakic, that all weapons must be surrendered by Hambarine and in surrounding villages. Failure would mean that the Serb forces would open fire, as was stated, with all available means. The decision was taken by those in Hambarine not to comply with the ultimatum, and accordingly, on the 23rd of May of 1992, the series of attacks began. Hambarine was shelled by artillery. Civilian houses were fired upon by tanks and there was targeting of the mosques. After the artillery shelling, troops, consisting of the military, the police, and paramilitary units, moved into the area the following day. They then systematically looted houses and set them on fire. Occupants were robbed. Many were killed. And those who fled were pursued and killed or captured. This attack, as I said, was just the first of many which took place in the municipality. Kozarac was given, the village, the town of Kozarac, was given the same type of ultimatum: Render your weapons. On the 24th of May, it was shelled for almost two days. The shelling was followed again by the entry of troops with the subsequent looting, killing, and rounding up of the population. The medical centre in Kozarac was itself apparently targeted. What happened in Kozarac came to exemplify to the outside world, the nature of those attacks in Prijedor as Omarska and Trnopolje were to exemplify the camps that were to be set up. In November of 1992, an American news organisation, ABC news, carried a programme called "Bosnia, the Hidden Horrors," and it sent a reporter to the Kozarac area in November of that year. And if we can just have a look at a short clip from that programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: ... a village in Northern Bosnia, an area dominated by ... (inaudible) in Prijedor and Banja Luka and a once thriving Muslim town called Kozarac. We visited the ethically cleansed Kozarac in northern Bosnia last week. We were closely supervised by the local Serb militia ... (inaudible) once home to about 15.000 Muslim men, women, and children. Today there are no Muslims there ... (inaudible) other homes in Kozarac have been marked to survive. This one with the colours of the Serbian flag. This one says: This is Serbian. They stand undamaged like the remaining Serb residents of Kozarac, surrounded in silence, deadly silence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution say that what that reporter had to say was correct that houses that were marked as Serb survived. Those that were not were destroyed, either through the shelling or what took place after that. At that same time, around the 24th of May, another predominantly Muslim village called Kamicani was also attacked. Houses were burnt and at least eight unarmed Muslim men and women were killed. Some resistance was put up to these attacks, but it was negligible. The Muslims and Croats had limited weaponry, and the force used against these villages was out of all proportion to the level of resistance which was or could have been offered. Presumably as a result of these attacks, on the 31st of May, a small resistance group consisting of roughly - and this comes from figures from interrogations carried out by the Serbs - roughly a hundred or so people attempted to retake the town of Prijedor. It was doomed to failure. The attack was easily repulsed by the Serb military and police units, but it provided the perfect excuse for the Serb authorities to accelerate the campaign to rid the area, the area of Prijedor town, of the non-Serb population. That area was a place called Stari Grad. I'm going to ask -- I don't think Your Honours have had yet a copy of the town plan of Prijedor which was got some photographs with it. Perhaps Your Honours can be handed that. Your Honours will see -- I'm sorry. I'm just trying to check where exactly on the town plan. I think, but I'm open to correction. Oh, yes, I'm sorry. We can see it marked. If Your Honours look at the plan, you'll see it's along the river that went through Prijedor, near the sports hall, and there's an aerial photograph. It was -- Stari Grad means "old town." And immediately following the attack on Prijedor, non-Serb men, women, and children were arrested and taken to detention facilities. Buildings were looted and burned again. Mosques were attacked. And most of that part of Stari Grad was effectively destroyed. Every single mosque in Prijedor was destroyed. The attacks - and I'm sorry, I should tell Your Honour that with the exception of the photograph of Stari Grad, most of these photographs that you see there were taken over the last 18 months or so, so they're not photographs of the place at the time. The attacks continued through the summer of 1992. A large number of those attacks took place in July of 1992 against both Muslim and Croat areas. The pattern of those attacks was the same as those which had taken place in May and June, the shelling, followed by the entry of troops, burning, looting, arrests, killings. The attacks were physically carried out by members of the military, the police, paramilitary formations, and to a certain extent people who were simply Serbs and had attached themselves to these formations. The actual orders to send the troops in within the system that existed at that time could only have been given within the military chain of command, and from the 22nd of May of 1992, Prijedor came within the command of General Talic and the 1st Krajina Corps. However, it is clear from the evidence that the military and political authorities were acting together. They shared the same objectives. The actual orders to go in came through the military chain of command, but the initiative, we suggest, in many cases, if not all, came from the political. And the aim, as I say, the objective, was shared by both or all police, military, political, whatever. It was to eradicate, to remove the non-Serb population from the municipality. Those who were not killed were detained, and so let me turn now to the camps. During the course of the spring and summer of 1992 up until the end of August, thousands of non-Serbs - men, women, and children, those under the age of 18, who were driven from their homes before and after attacks - were taken to, as I said earlier, one of these detention, collection, whatever, centres, in other words, camps. Of these camps, the most notorious were, of course, Omarska, which was established in a mining complex just outside Prijedor, of which you can see an overhead view on the map which you've just been handed; Keraterm, established in an old ceramics factory in Prijedor itself, and again, you can see an old photograph of that camp, photograph 7; and Trnopolje, a village that was close to Kozarac. You can see that in photograph 5. The camps were set up as a result of the direct orders issued by the Prijedor Crisis Staff. If you look at document 200, this is the official order dated the 31st of May, 1992. It's, in actual fact, on this occasion signed by the chief of public security, Simo Drljaca, and it says, in item 1, that: "The industrial compound of the Omarska mines strip shall serve as a provisional collection centre for persons captured in combat or detained on the grounds of the security services' operational information." Unlike the recordings that were made during the Second World War of what was to happen, the documents produced by the Serbs in the course of this operation are much more anodyne. They don't actually set out in terms what is intended. And where it's stated that a provisional collection centre for persons captured in combat or detained on the grounds of security services operational information, the suggestion presumably being those who were actually fighting or those whom the police had reason to believe were in some way aiding and abetting resistance or combatants. In actual fact, the majority of people who ended up in Omarska were civilians, including women, and the rest of the document deals with what is to happen. In paragraph 9: "Authorised representatives of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovinia shall without delay, lay a mine field in accordance with the mining regulations," et cetera. And at paragraph 15: "I most strictly prohibit giving any information whatsoever concerning the functioning of this collection centre. All official documents shall be kept at the collection centre and may be taken out or destroyed only with the permission of the Chief of the Prijedor public security station." It's not surprising that there was prohibition on giving out information of the functioning. Now, that order is dated the 31st of May. In fact, the Omarska camp went into operation some days earlier. And from its first days, it housed many of what were considered to be the leaders of the Muslim and Croat populations: Lawyers, engineers, teachers, a judge. The Muslim president of the Assembly, sometimes known as the mayor, Muhamed Cehajic was arrested by the police on the 23rd of May. He was detained for a few days at the police station, of which you can also see a photograph in photograph 2 on the map, and then taken to Omarska. At Omarska, he was deliberately, it would appear, targeted for severe beatings. Other witnesses saw him being called out by the guards. Eventually he was taken from Omarska, in late July, together with other people considered to be leaders of the communities. He has never been seen since that day. In Omarska there was savage beatings during and -- out with interrogations. These were commonplace. Murders took place on a virtual daily basis, either through execution, by shooting, or deaths as a result of the beatings. And from about mid-July, the number of killings increased. Bodies were seen in the morning prior to being loaded onto trucks and then removed. Women who were at the camp were raped or otherwise sexually assaulted. The general conditions of life in that camp were atrocious. Persons detained were given starvation rations, polluted water. They were kept in severely overcrowded conditions, with no bedding, no change of clothes, and wholly inadequate medical care. Records kept by the Serbs themselves show that between the 27th of May and the 16th of August, 1992, a total of some 3.334 persons were taken to Omarska, and those included 37 women, 28 persons under the age of 18, and 68 over the age of 60. None of those could even remotely be regarded as combatants or people capable of combat. Many of those people who passed through Omarska remain unaccounted for. Many bodies have been subsequently exhumed from mass grave sites. And Omarska was only finally disbanded on the 21st of August, really as a result of the furore caused by the film taken by the international journalists who were allowed, no doubt later regretted, by Karadzic, to visit. Those prisoners were then transferred, were transferred to Manjaca, a military-run camp outside Banja Luka. Keraterm. That began operating on or about the 23rd of May, and conditions therein were similar to those that pertained in Omarska: Wholly inadequate facilities, water, food, hygiene. On arrival at the camp, any property which the prisoners had, was removed and they were beaten before being forced into four storage rooms which had metal doors, and this was the summer months in Bosnia. The majority of the prisoners in Keraterm were called for interrogation at some time during their incarceration, and again, interrogations carried out by the police included beatings and torture at a regular feature. Again, outside the interrogations, there were beatings and sexual assaults carried out not only by camp guards but also by outsiders who were allowed in to the premises of Keraterm. And again, as with Omarska, particular attention was paid to persons considered to be political or civic leaders, intellectuals, or just plain richer than anybody else. Keraterm, as is now well known, was the site of one of the largest mass killings in the municipality. On about the 20th of July, a substantial number, something in the region of a hundred Muslims, were transported from the Brdo region. And again, if you look at the map, you can see where that is. It includes Biscani, Hambarine, and the like - to Keraterm. They were confined in one of the rooms, room 3, and during the evening of the 24th of July, a number of armed and uniformed Serbs opened fire on the occupants with machine-guns. Somewhere between 150 and 200 civilians died. That killing spree was repeated the following night. On this occasion, about 40 people died. And like Omarska, Keraterm was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. disbanded, although earlier than Omarska, sometime at the beginning of August. About Keraterm, there can be no doubt, no dispute as to what the regime was, because the camp commander, a man called Sikirica, and various people who were tried earlier at this court, pleaded guilty at the 11th hour, as it were, to conduct that was persecutory in nature and which included killings outside that of Room 3. About the third major camp, Trnopolje. It fell into a slightly different category in that there was a certain freedom for the inmates to enter and leave. However, again, conditions at the camp were inhumane. They were cramped, there was no electricity, and little available food. And again, there were beatings, sexual assaults, and killings committed both by guards and by people who were allowed in from the outside. The camp commander was a Major Kuruzovic, who Your Honours saw his name as an original member of the Prijedor Crisis Staff, head of the municipal territorial organisation before it was absorbed into the Bosnian Serb army. And Trnopolje, as it were, saw the starting point for events that led perhaps to the worst of all the massacres in the area. On or about the 21st of August, a number of the male detainees were told that they would be sent to a Muslim-held territory for exchange. These men were placed on buses. As the buses drove over an area known as Mount Vlasic, they stopped. The men were taken off, and something like 200 men were massacred. Only a handful survived. Some were killed by shooting, some as they were pushed or fell over the cliffs, the ravine that is typical of that part of the world. Responsible for that massacre were members of the police. In July of 1992, some Muslim men from Biscani had been brought to Trnopolje. Some were left on the bus that was transporting them there. That bus drove off, and later those men were killed. At its peak, the camp held thousands of non-Serb civilians, and in August of 1992, hundreds were loaded onto buses and trucks and removed to other parts of Bosnia or out of the country, to places like Croatia, and from then on to other European countries. It was these camps that brought the attention to the outside world as to what was happening in Prijedor and really made it infamous, and it is worth having a look at a short clip from the news item that was broadcast by ITN in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These are the Muslim prisoners of Omarska. In small groups under heavy Serbian guard they are ushered into the canteen for their single meal of the day. Most have been here for two months ... (inaudible) rounded up from their homes. They were too frightened to talk about the way they have been treated and the conditions in which they have been kept, conditions which have been hidden from the world as the Serbs have denied access here to the United Nations and to the International Red Cross. Their prison is an old mining complex outside Banja Luka in northern Bosnia. In an office above the canteen, the camp commandant and the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause the video for just one moment. The man standing there talking through the interpreter was the chief of police, Simo Drljaca. Yes, if we could go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They had two and a half thousand of what they called internees who were being interrogated as possible Muslim fighters. No, this is not a camp. This is a centre, a private centre ... (inaudible). The prisoners were being brought to the canteen from the large industrial building in the centre of the mining complex. It too was under heavy guard and we asked to be allowed to look inside. But in spite of promises of openness from the Serb Bosnian leader, Dr. Karadzic, we were told we could see no more. Why are you not considering ... (inaudible) We can do this and this and that and not that. Our armed escort made it clear our visit was over. We are now being asked to leave this camp having seen nothing more than the canteen. We are being told that Dr. Karadzic's promise, while good to us, does not carry any weight here. As we were moved on, soldiers told us the army did not control the camp which they said was run by the local authorities and militia. We had asked to be taken to a second camp, but Trnopolje, in the same area, to which several hundred prisoners from Omarska had that day been transferred and which has also been at the centre of allegation of atrocities. Conditions at this camp were appalling. In 100-degree heat, hundreds of men were forced to eat and sleep outside in a field behind barbed wire. Their meager rations consist of a small hunk of bread and a bowl of soup every day. Here too they simply have been rounded up, whole villages emptied of their men and they were afraid. Can you tell me anything about the conditions in which you are being kept? I'm not sure that I'm allowed about that, you know. Can you understand me? People here have been beaten? Here? No. Here, no. Here. (Inaudible). I rather wouldn't talk about that. Can you tell us anything about the conditions that you were being kept in and the treatment of the people you were with? Well, that was (inaudible). We heard stories of people being beaten and (inaudible). Did that happen? You just came here from another camp. From another camp. We accept a little bit more better, like. What was it like before? Oh, it was terrible. One of the prisoners asked us to check on him in several days' time to see that he hadn't been punished for speaking to us, and away from the camera, there were allegations of routine beatings and executions. Several prisoners told us of retaliatory killings. One instance in which they claimed 150 of their fellow prisoners had been killed following the death of ten Serbian soldiers in a Muslim village. We were told people had been beaten to death and we were asked to smuggle a film out of the camp. The pictures show severe injuries, apparently as a result of beatings. In the makeshift medical centre, there were cases of scabies, malnutrition and diarrhoea. Local doctors said they were chronically short of medicines and drugs. Among them was a Muslim doctor. We asked him whether there had been any cases of beatings. (Inaudible). On one side of the camp were refugees who were here simply because they have nowhere else to go, their homes having been destroyed. They have been told they can go as soon as they have a guarantee of a home outside Serb-controlled Bosnia. In Banja Luka, prisoners' wives have been queueing for days for news of their men and to register as refugees, because they too have nowhere to go. Muslim villages lie empty and deserted, homes destroyed. If there is eventually freedom for the men in the detention centres, it's unlikely to be in Serb-controlled Bosnia. Ian Williams, ITN, Northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. What you may have missed, what Kovacevic -- I'm sorry. What you may have missed, what Kovacevic was saying, member of the Crisis Staff, was that people had lost control, as he put it. Those camps were the worst, the most notorious, but there were others. In the village of Ljubija, a football stadium in which Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats were detained, beaten, and killed. On the 26th of July, over a hundred Muslim men were captured near Ravska. Some who tried to escape were killed. Those detained were taken to the Serb headquarters at Miska Glava, interrogated, and beaten, and the next day a number were killed. The survivors were taken to the football stadium. There they were beaten and more were murdered. And there were people detained at the Prijedor police station, which you can see, the SUP, the S-U-P, in photograph 2, and the JNA military barracks which you can see in photographs 8, and in particular, 9. And again, in all these places, the same cycle, the same pattern was repeated of beatings during and outside interrogations. So what were the results of the policies pursued? The attacks and killings resulted in the deaths of thousands. Over 1.000 bodies have been recovered through exhumations which were carried out and are still being carried out today. Over a thousand declarations of death have been issued by the Bosnian courts in respect of people who were missing, believed killed in the Prijedor region. The Serbs' own documentation shows that between about April 1992 and the 16th of August, when the report was prepared, something in the region of 20.000 non-Serbs left the municipality of Prijedor, either driven out by fear, but in the main, forcibly expelled by the Serbs. By June of 1993, when the Serbs were making an estimate - none of these were perfect, because there wasn't a census - the Muslim population of 49.000 people-odd had been reduced to just over 6.000, and the Croat population, which was much smaller, had effectively halved. The Serb authorities achieved in Prijedor more than in almost any other municipality, particularly in the area, exactly what they intended, namely, the almost complete eradication of the non-Serb population. The Prijedor Serb authorities, headed by the accused, desired this result, but effectively on their own terms. It wasn't enough to create conditions of life that would make it impossible for non-Serbs to remain. In one sense, the authorities made it as difficult as possible for non-Serbs to leave voluntarily, if that's the right word. They were made to pay to leave. They were made to sign over their property. Their property was in fact confiscated after they left. Transportation was limited. And it could be said that the authorities turned Prijedor into one giant concentration camp from which persons were only able to escape if they avoided death or serious injury at the will of the authorities and on their terms deported in buses and trucks used for exchanges and the like. The concentration of the deliberate killings was on what were considered to be the leaders of the Muslims and the Croats. Really, the old saying, "Cut off the head and the body withers" was applied to what happened in Prijedor. Prijedor wasn't Srebrenica, but effectively, what was achieved by a series of attacks, by mass executions, by deaths from beatings and torture, was to destroy, at least in part, the Muslim and Croat population of Prijedor. Finally, what was the role and responsibility of Stakic for the events that I've just described? Milomir Stakic was born in 1962. By the time of these events, he had qualified as a medical doctor. His age and profession could be said to make his role in these events even more disgraceful than most. The positions held by him, as President of the Crisis Staff, head of the Municipal Council for National defence, gave him a very real and not illusory authority. Yugoslavia, Bosnia, Prijedor still operated under the apparatus and to a certain extent the ideology of a rigid communist system, whereby the state controlled all aspects of life and all who participated in these events in 1992, either as victim or perpetrator, had grown up under this system. Stakic was intimately involved in the events immediately prior to the seizure of power by the SDS in Prijedor. It would seem from the documentation that is available that within the Prijedor SDS, there was something of a power struggle before the takeover occurred, and it was Stakic who played a major role in the removal of the then leader of the local SDS, a man named Srdic. He was involved in an attempt to set up a Serb municipality surrounding the Omarska area, and the Prosecution say that his activities prior to the takeover show that this was a man committed to, as I say, Serb ideology, to the policies of the SDS. This was no mere fellow traveller or figurehead. His role in the takeover itself, his visit to Prijedor Radio, the announcement that was made of the takeover of power, and the reasons, or one of the reasons he gave was that Muslims should not be allowed to take part in the government of the municipality because Prijedor was Serbian land. Stakic exerted his authority immediately after the takeover. The Muslim leader of the legally elected Municipal Assembly was officially removed in a letter signed by Stakic. His subsequent arrest and incarceration, which I've already dealt with, could not have taken place given the position of this man without the authority of the head of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor. We've looked at the list of persons who composed the Crisis Staff. They were those who, by virtue of their jobs, were able to exert the necessary authority, the president of the assembly and the like, and to put into effect the decisions taken. Now, although there were no military representatives shown as former members, records show a regular attendance by Colonel Arsic and Major Zeljaja, at meetings either of the Crisis Staff or the Council for National Defence, which was also presided over by the accused. The Office of the Prosecutor has acquired a short video clip. I have to say it's not all together clear when it was taken, but it would appear sometime in 1992, and would appear to be showing a meeting of the Crisis Staff. Now, the commentary is in the Bosnian language, and I hope that Your Honours have been given the transcript of what's being said. And I wonder if that could now be played.

utterances.text: Pausing there. Not altogether and on this I stand to be contradicted, but it is thought that one of the two men in military uniform sitting there is Colonel Arsic. But as I say, I'm open -- we had some difficulty in making the identification. Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] While the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Pause. We'll come to the final ... What is being said there by the journalist, of course, is that power was taken over in Prijedor, and the joining of the municipality with the Autonomous Region of Krajina. What sort of decisions were being taken and signed off upon by the Prijedor Crisis Staff and Stakic? Just about as one saw from the list of tasks and duties that was shown on the instructions to the local Crisis Staff, every aspect of life. Decisions leading to the dismissal of non-Serbs. Somebody was watching and says sorry, it wasn't Arsic, it was Zeljaja, the gentleman in the military uniform. Decisions in respect of the police, in respect of the dealings with prisoners, the setting up of camps, establishment of the local crisis staffs, declarations that property which was "abandoned" should become state property, in other words, authorised theft. The Prijedor Crisis Staff ruled the lives of the area -- of the persons in the area during this period. And what did Stakic himself have to say about this matter? He gave an interview to a newspaper in 1994, and it's document 423 - in which the headline -- the allegation making that the SDA, the Muslim nationalist party had a detailed plan for the liquidation of Serbs. They were secretly arming themselves, making up uniforms with the "lily" symbols and building strongholds in Kozara and neighbouring districts. This was part of the propaganda that was put out at the time and continued throughout. And the interviewer quotes Stakic as about halfway down the page, one sees the words, he said, "This is what he said at the start of our interview, 'What happened on the 30th of April, 1992 was only the final act of a long-standing but for the Serbs perilous plan. I often talked in private with the leaders of the SDA and the HDZ, and this is what convinced me that they were concocting a terrible plan regarding the Serbs, secretly arming themselves, making uniforms with the symbol of the "lily", building strongholds in Kozara. But we were not just sitting there with our hands in our laps. When we saw what we were doing, we began to arm ourselves and to tell party members that what they were planning to do to us and what has to be done to prevent 1941 happening all over again. On the direction of the central office of the SDS, we formed the Serbian assembly of Prijedor and I became chairman.'" And then at the bottom of the page: "In April, things started to happen in Sarajevo, Bosanska Krupa and other places, and this convinced us that we have to speed up the process of arming ourselves." Then it talks about an all-party conference and then this at the bottom of the page: "I was informed through my own channels that a decision had also been reached to take over power by force, and we were lucky that Colonel Arsic was the commander of our garrison, a good soldier and a man with a lot of experience, and we decided to speed up the process of arming ourselves." He then deals with the Serb version of what caused the attack on Kozarac, and says this: "When we took into custody the most hardened of extremists, continued Mr. Stakic, we gathered enough information to conclude that the Muslims were well organised and determined to liquidate their fellow citizens, the Serbs." And it goes on repeating this plan that it was said that the Muslims had for the liquidation of the Serbian population, and then at the last sentence of that paragraph: "But we stopped them, and in doing so, prevented the repeat of the massacre of the Second World War." Finally, we would invite Your Honours to look at a clip of an interview with Stakic that was conducted, it would appear, in 1992. If they could play the final part of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKIC

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There can be no greater travesty of the truth of what happened in Omarska than what Stakic had to say about it. Your Honours, at the end of the day, as I say, you will decide on the evidence you've heard from the witnesses and from the documents, where the truth, as you are enjoined in this case, lies, but the Prosecution suggests to you, in the strongest possible terms, that having examined that evidence, you can be satisfied so that you are sure that this accused, Milomir Stakic, was directly responsible for the events that took place in Prijedor between April and September of 1992.
